short: This site's letter for how strong the evidence behind a health statement is: A (pooled human trials) down to E (laboratory only), or T for traditional use in an official monograph.
definition: A label attached to every health statement on this site. A means a systematic review or meta-analysis of human randomised controlled trials; B at least one human randomised trial; C observational or small uncontrolled human studies; D animal studies; E laboratory (in vitro) or computer (in silico) studies; T traditional use recorded in an official monograph. A grade always belongs to a named test article, never to a plant in general.

short: The exact thing a study tested: whole herb, a named extract, an essential oil, an isolated compound or a multi-herb formula. A grade belongs to its test article only.
definition: The material actually given or applied in a study. An enteric-coated peppermint-oil capsule, a peppermint tea and pure menthol are three different test articles, and evidence about one says nothing direct about the others. This site records the test article next to every grade so that a strong result for an oil capsule is not read as a result for a cup of tea.

short: A specific manufactured extract (solvent, plant-to-extract ratio, often a code name) used in a trial. Its results do not transfer automatically to other extracts or to tea.
definition: An extract made by a defined process, often sold or coded under a name, and sometimes standardised to contain a set amount of a marker compound. Two extracts of the same plant made with different solvents can contain different molecules, so a trial result is attached to that extract alone.

short: Test article meaning the dried or fresh plant material itself (or a simple preparation of it), rather than an extract, oil or pure compound.
definition: The plant part as harvested, dried or powdered, including simple preparations such as a tea. Evidence graded against whole herb is the closest this site comes to evidence about the plant as grown, but it still depends on how the herb was prepared.

short: Test article meaning a single purified molecule (e.g. pure menthol), not the plant or an extract containing it.
definition: A single chemical substance purified or synthesised and tested on its own. Results for an isolated compound say what the molecule can do at the tested concentration; they do not say that a plant containing it, or a tea made from that plant, delivers enough of it.

short: Test article made of several plants combined (e.g. Sho-saiko-to, thyme + ivy syrup). Its evidence belongs to the combination, not to any one ingredient.
definition: A product combining two or more herbs. Traditional Japanese and Chinese formulas and many European cough syrups are of this kind. Because the ingredients cannot be separated after the fact, this site grades the formula and never transfers the grade to a single plant in it.

short: A study in which people are assigned by chance to the treatment or a comparison (often placebo), so that differences in outcome can be attributed to the treatment.
definition: The standard design for testing whether an intervention works in people. Random assignment balances known and unknown differences between groups; blinding (double-blind: neither participants nor assessors know who got what) and a placebo control reduce bias further. One RCT gives grade B on this site; a meta-analysis of several gives grade A.

short: An inactive look-alike given to the comparison group of a trial, so that expectation effects are the same in both groups.
definition: A dummy treatment with no active ingredient, made to look, smell or taste like the real one. In herbal trials a convincing placebo is hard to make for strongly flavoured preparations such as peppermint oil or sage.

short: A trial in which each participant receives both the treatment and the comparison in turn, in random order, so each person is their own control.
definition: Useful for short-acting effects and small samples, such as single-dose cognition studies or drug-interaction studies. Its weakness is carry-over: the first treatment can still be acting when the second begins.

short: A study in which everyone knows what treatment is being given; there is no blinding and often no control group. Graded C on this site.
definition: Open-label studies are easier to run but vulnerable to expectation and to improvement that would have happened anyway. Many herbal studies are of this kind, which is one reason they sit at grade C rather than B.

short: A study that records what people already do or experience, without assigning a treatment. It can show association, not cause. Graded C here.
definition: Cohort, case-control and cross-sectional studies watch rather than intervene. Because people who choose a herb differ in other ways from those who do not, an association is weak evidence of an effect. A meta-analysis of observational studies is still C on this site.

short: A published description of one patient (or a small series) with an unusual event, such as liver injury after a herbal product. Signals a possible harm; does not measure its risk.
definition: Case reports are how most herbal adverse effects first come to light. They cannot show how often the harm occurs and are easily confounded by other products, contamination or adulteration, which is why the skullcap and chamomile safety blocks treat them with care.

short: A statistical pooling of the results of several studies of the same question, giving one overall estimate. Pooled human RCTs give grade A here.
definition: Meta-analysis combines effect estimates across studies, weighting larger and more precise ones more heavily. It is only as good as the studies pooled: combining trials of different test articles produces a number that describes none of them.

short: A review that searches for every study on a question using stated methods and criteria, so the selection itself is not biased.
definition: Unlike a narrative review, a systematic review publishes its search, inclusion rules and quality appraisal. It may or may not end in a meta-analysis. A systematic review of trials of mixed sage preparations can conclude that the evidence is weak even where the individual trials were positive.

short: Studies in test tubes, dishes or isolated cells and receptors, outside a living organism. Graded E here and never phrased as an effect in people.
definition: In vitro work shows what a molecule can do at a given concentration in a controlled system. Concentrations used are often far higher than anything reached in the blood after eating or drinking a plant. Computer (in silico) predictions such as docking share grade E.

short: An experiment in living animals, usually rats or mice. Graded D here: it can show a mechanism or a hazard but is never phrased as an effect in people.
definition: Animal studies supply most toxicity data, including the rodent studies behind the EMA limits for thujone, pulegone and estragole. Doses are often far above human exposure, and species differ in metabolism.

short: A use accepted by a regulator because a herb has been used safely that way for a long time (EMA: at least 30 years), not because trials proved it works. Graded T here.
definition: The EMA registers traditional herbal medicinal products on evidence of long-standing use and plausibility rather than clinical efficacy. This site reports such a statement as "traditionally used for", attributed to the monograph, and never as "helps" or "treats".

short: EMA category for a herbal medicine whose efficacy and safety are supported by published scientific data, as opposed to traditional use alone.
definition: A higher bar than traditional use. The EMA accepts well-established use for enteric-coated peppermint oil in irritable bowel symptoms, but it rejected it for sage because the products tested in trials did not match products on the EU market.

short: The European Medicines Agency's Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products, which writes assessment reports and monographs on herbs and their constituents of concern.
definition: The HMPC reviews the literature on a herb and publishes an assessment report (the evidence) and an EU herbal monograph (the conclusions), plus public statements on risky constituents such as thujone, pulegone, estragole and methyleugenol. Its documents are the anchor sources of this site.

short: An official summary of what a regulator or expert body accepts about a herb: indications, preparations, contraindications and warnings.
definition: Monographs are published by the EMA HMPC, ESCOP, the WHO and (historically) Germany's Commission E. A monograph listing a traditional use is the basis of grade T on this site; its posology is never repeated as advice.

short: The official book of quality standards for medicines in Europe. It sets minimum contents, e.g. of thymol + carvacrol in thyme oil or of rosmarinic acid in lemon balm.
definition: Pharmacopoeial monographs define what a herbal drug must contain to be sold as that drug. They are quality specifications, not evidence of effect, but they are a useful statement of what typical material contains.

short: A free NIH database of drug- and supplement-induced liver injury, with case summaries and a likelihood score for each agent. The skullcap safety block draws on it.
definition: LiverTox is maintained by the US National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases and hosted on the NCBI Bookshelf. Its entries for herbal products discuss adulteration and multi-ingredient products alongside the herb itself.

short: Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry: separates the volatile molecules of an oil and identifies each by its mass spectrum. The source of most essential-oil percentages.
definition: The oil is vaporised and carried through a long column; each compound leaves at a characteristic time and is then fragmented and identified. Results are usually given as a percentage of the total peak area, i.e. per cent of the oil, not of the leaf.

short: High-performance liquid chromatography: separates dissolved, non-volatile molecules such as rosmarinic acid or baicalin so they can be measured.
definition: The workhorse method for phenolic acids and flavonoid glycosides in extracts, teas and tinctures. Results are typically reported per gram of dry plant, per gram of extract or per millilitre of liquid.

short: Area under the plasma concentration-time curve: the total exposure of the body to a drug. An interaction that lowers AUC means less drug reached the blood.
definition: Pharmacokinetic studies measure a drug in blood over time and integrate the curve; Cmax is the peak of that curve. Comparing AUC with and without a herb constituent, as in the baicalin-rosuvastatin study, is how interactions are quantified.

short: A regulator's figure for how much of a constituent of concern a person may be exposed to per day without special concern. A safety threshold, not a recommended amount.
definition: Guidance values for estragole, thujone and pulegone + menthofuran appear in the safety blocks. They are derived from animal toxicology: the highest dose with no observed adverse effect (NOAEL), or a benchmark dose modelled from the dose-response curve, divided by uncertainty factors. They are precautionary and stated for herbal medicinal products, not culinary use.

short: Milligrams per kilogram of body weight: a dose scaled to the size of the person or animal.
definition: Toxicological limits are usually given per kilogram of body weight per day, then multiplied by a reference weight (often 50 or 60 kg) to give a per-person figure.

short: Parts per million: 1 ppm is 1 mg per kg. 10,000 ppm = 1 %. Dr. Duke's reports most values in ppm, often without saying of what (leaf, oil or plant).
definition: A ppm value means nothing until its basis is known: 10,000 ppm of the oil is 1 % of the oil, but 10,000 ppm of the dry leaf is 1 % of the leaf, a far larger amount. The catalogue carries a basis on every value for that reason.

short: What an amount is 'per': fresh weight, dry weight, per cent of essential oil or per gram of extract. Values on different bases are never compared on this site.
definition: The same compound can be 40 % of an oil and 0.5 % of the leaf the oil came from. A number without its basis cannot be compared with anything, so every occurrence row carries one and the compare view refuses to mix them.

short: Amount per gram of plant as harvested, water included. Fresh leaves are mostly water, so fresh-weight values are much lower than dry-weight values for the same plant.
definition: Leaves are commonly 70-90 % water, so converting between fresh and dry weight needs the water content of that sample, which is often not reported. The site does not convert; it shows the basis as published.

short: Amount per gram of dried plant material. The usual basis for phenolics and flavonoids measured by HPLC.
definition: Drying removes water but can also change the chemistry: carnosic acid oxidises to carnosol, and oven-drying lowered chamomile phenolics. A dry-weight value therefore describes dried material, not the living plant.

short: An amount expressed as a share of the distilled oil, not of the plant. Thymol at 50 % of thyme oil may be well under 1 % of the dry leaf.
definition: GC-MS reports the composition of the oil itself. Because oil is typically a few per cent of the plant at most, a large percentage of the oil is a small amount of the leaf, and says nothing about what reaches a water infusion.

short: An amount relative to an extract after solvent removal. It depends on how much else the solvent pulled out, so it cannot be converted back to the plant.
definition: Extracts concentrate some constituents and exclude others; 406 mg baicalin per gram of an aqueous root extract is a statement about the extract, not about the root.

short: One catalogue row saying that a compound was reported in a species' plant part, with amount, basis, source and a verified flag.
definition: An occurrence links a compound to a greenhouse species. It is species-level unless the source names a cultivar, and it never implies that the greenhouse's own plants were measured.

short: Whether the greenhouse entry's species is confirmed, needs checking, or is unresolved (skullcap: S. lateriflora or S. baicalensis?).
definition: Recorded on every inventory entry. An unresolved entry is profiled under each candidate species side by side and resolves by changing a single field once the plant is identified.

short: A molecule formed by handling rather than by the living plant, e.g. carnosol from carnosic acid on drying, chamazulene from matricin on steam distillation.
definition: Artefacts matter because a compound reported in dried herb or in an oil may not exist in the fresh plant, and the reverse.

short: A cultivated variety selected and named by growers, e.g. 'Genovese' basil. Chemistry can differ sharply between cultivars of one species.
definition: The greenhouse grows several basil cultivars whose oils are of different chemotypes. This site uses cultivar-level data only when a source names the cultivar, and flags that it is the study's plant, not the greenhouse's.

short: A rank below species for a distinct population, e.g. Origanum vulgare subsp. hirtum (Greek oregano). Databases do not always agree on subspecies.
definition: POWO, GBIF and NCBI sometimes treat the same subspecies differently, which is why each taxon page states which rank the identifiers belong to.

short: The × in a name such as Mentha × piperita marks a hybrid: peppermint is a cross between water mint and spearmint.
definition: Hybrid names carry a multiplication sign before the epithet. Hybrids are often propagated by cuttings, so a named clone can be chemically uniform while the hybrid as a whole varies.

short: A group of closely related species treated together under one name because they are hard to tell apart.
definition: Some herbal literature reports results for an aggregate rather than a single species, which weakens any claim about one species.

short: The scientific name a taxonomic authority currently recognises for a species; older names become synonyms (e.g. Rosmarinus officinalis is now Salvia rosmarinus).
definition: This site takes accepted names from POWO and lists synonyms so that older literature can be matched to the right plant.

short: The mint family: basil, mints, lemon balm, sage, rosemary, thyme, oregano and skullcap. Aromatic oils in surface glands; rosmarinic acid widespread.
definition: The best-represented family in the greenhouse and the focus of the prototype's profiles.

short: The daisy family, including chamomile, ragweed and lettuce. Relevant here for allergy cross-reactivity.
definition: People allergic to one member, especially ragweed, may react to others such as chamomile; the chamomile safety block carries this.

short: Plants of the World Online, the Royal Botanic Gardens Kew database of accepted plant names; the source of accepted names and POWO ids here.
definition: POWO identifiers are IPNI name identifiers (urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:...). The site links each taxon to its POWO record.

short: The Global Biodiversity Information Facility: an international species and occurrence database; its API supplied name matches and GBIF keys.
definition: GBIF also mirrors other checklists, including NCBI Taxonomy, which is how this prototype read NCBI taxids when NCBI itself was unreachable.

short: The numeric identifier of an organism in the NCBI Taxonomy database, used to link a plant to its gene and sequence records.
definition: NCBI's classification is built for sequence databases and does not always match botanical treatments; it may keep a subspecies that POWO sinks.

short: The compound identifier in PubChem, the NIH open chemistry database. Each compound record here links to its CID.
definition: A CID refers to one specific structure; stereoisomers and mixtures (such as citral) can have separate CIDs, so the record notes which was used.

short: A fixed-length 27-character code computed from a structure, used to match the same molecule across databases.
definition: The first block encodes the connectivity; the second, stereochemistry and isotopes. Two records with the same InChIKey are the same compound.

short: A line of text that encodes a molecular structure (e.g. linalool: CC(=CCCC(C)(C=C)O)C). The site draws every structure from its SMILES.
definition: Simplified Molecular-Input Line-Entry System. SMILES strings here were retrieved from PubChem and are recomputed at build time.

short: Chemical Entities of Biological Interest: an ontology of small molecules; ChEBI ids link compounds to biological databases.
definition: Where a ChEBI id could not be confirmed it is left empty rather than guessed.

short: One of two mirror-image forms of a molecule. They can smell and act differently; basil linalool is usually reported as the (R)-(-) form.
definition: Databases often hold a stereo-unspecified record; where the plant's form was not confirmed, the record says so.

variants: Dr. Duke's Phytochemical and Ethnobotanical Databases
short: The USDA database of plant chemicals compiled by James Duke; a source of occurrence rows, often in ppm with the plant part but not always the basis.
definition: Duke's rows cite older literature and are used here only when a readable source paper supports them.

short: A Japanese database of species-metabolite relationships; used here to confirm that a compound has been reported from a species.
definition: KNApSAcK lists presence, not amounts, and entries can be ambiguous (its 'wogonin 7-glucoside' is not wogonoside).

short: The natural-products occurrence database (lotus.naturalproducts.net) linking structures to the organisms they were reported from, with references.
definition: Used for presence checks; several responses were truncated during the sweep, which is recorded in the gaps.

short: A linear polymer of glucose that forms the load-bearing fibres of plant cell walls; the most abundant biopolymer on Earth.
definition: Cellulose chains bundle into microfibrils that resist turgor pressure, the outward push of the cell's contents; they are spun at the cell surface by membrane complexes of cellulose synthase (CESA) subunits guided by microtubules. The wall stays in the strainer when a tea is made.

short: Hemicelluloses and pectins: the branched and gel-forming polysaccharides that make up the hydrated matrix around cellulose in the primary cell wall.
definition: Hemicelluloses such as xyloglucan coat and link cellulose microfibrils; pectins, rich in galacturonic acid, hold water and help cells adhere. Growth proteins called expansins loosen the bonds between these polymers so the wall can yield to turgor pressure.

short: A family of plant organelles (chloroplasts among them) with their own metabolism; the site of the MEP pathway to monoterpenes and diterpenes.
definition: The chloroplast, where photosynthesis happens, is the best-known plastid. Plastids and the cytosol make isoprenoid building blocks by different routes, which is why terpene classes are split between compartments.

short: The fluid interior of the cell outside the organelles; the site of the mevalonate pathway to sesquiterpenes, sterols and triterpenes.
definition: Enzymes of many biosynthetic steps float in or are anchored at the edge of the cytosol.

short: The stacked internal membranes of the chloroplast that carry chlorophyll and the complexes of the light reactions.
definition: Photosystem II, the cytochrome b6f complex, photosystem I and ATP synthase sit in the thylakoid membrane.

short: A large protein-pigment complex that captures light. Photosystem II splits water and releases oxygen; photosystem I helps make NADPH.
definition: The two photosystems work in series along the thylakoid electron transport chain.

short: The two products of the light reactions: ATP, the cell's energy currency, and NADPH, its carrier of reducing power. Both pay for carbon fixation.
definition: In the chloroplast ATP is made by ATP synthase, driven by the proton gradient of the electron transport chain, and NADPH by photosystem I. Many biosynthetic enzymes on this site, such as basil's eugenol-forming reductase, are NADPH-dependent.

short: The enzyme that fixes CO2 into sugar in photosynthesis; slow, and confused by oxygen competing for its active site.
definition: Rubisco catalyses the first step of net carbon assimilation and is often the limit on photosynthesis. Every carbon atom in the herbs' oils and phenolics passed through it.

short: A compound not needed for basic growth that varies between lineages (terpenes, phenolics, alkaloids); plants use them in defence and signalling.
definition: Long treated as waste, secondary metabolites are now understood as part of a plant's survival strategy. Nearly every compound record on this site is one.

short: A tiny hair on the leaf surface that makes and stores essential oil. In the mints, oil sits in these glands, which is why rubbing the leaf releases the scent.
definition: Peltate trichomes of mint and basil are the site of menthol and estragole biosynthesis. Oil stored outside the leaf cells is volatile and partly lost on drying and heating.

short: The plastid route that makes the C5 terpenoid building blocks (IPP/DMAPP) from pyruvate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate; feeds monoterpenes and diterpenes.
definition: Discovered in the 1990s, it runs alongside the older-known mevalonate pathway. The split between the two is broad rather than absolute.

short: The cytosolic route from acetyl-CoA to the C5 terpenoid building blocks; feeds sesquiterpenes, sterols and triterpenes.
definition: Named after its intermediate mevalonic acid. Animals and fungi use it too; the MEP pathway is found in plastids and bacteria.

short: Isopentenyl diphosphate and dimethylallyl diphosphate: the two five-carbon units from which every terpenoid is assembled.
definition: Chains of two (C10), three (C15), four (C20) or six (C30) units give the monoterpenes, sesquiterpenes, diterpenes and triterpenes.

short: The ten-carbon precursor of every monoterpene; different terpene synthases fold it into menthol's, thymol's or camphor's skeleton.
definition: The choice of synthase, not the precursor, decides which monoterpenes a plant makes.

short: An enzyme that turns a prenyl diphosphate into a terpene skeleton. Its gene sets a plant's scent; one broken basil synthase changes linalool into geraniol.
definition: Terpene synthases form large gene families and often make several products at once.

short: A large family of oxidising enzymes. In plants they decorate terpene skeletons (thymol, ursolic acid); in the liver they metabolise drugs and can bioactivate toxins.
definition: The same enzyme family underlies two stories on this site: biosynthesis in the plant and bioactivation of pulegone, estragole and teucrin A in the body.

short: The liver and gut P450 enzyme that metabolises about half of prescription drugs; inhibiting it can raise drug levels.
definition: Peppermint oil inhibits CYP3A4 in vitro; whether that matters in people depends on exposure, which is why the interaction is graded E.

short: The route from phosphoenolpyruvate and erythrose 4-phosphate to the aromatic amino acids; at least 30 % of fixed carbon in vascular plants passes through it.
definition: It supplies phenylalanine and tyrosine, the starting points of the phenylpropanoid, flavonoid and rosmarinic-acid branches.

short: An enzyme that adds a methyl group to an oxygen. Two basil OMTs make estragole and methyleugenol; one amino acid decides which.
definition: Methylation often changes a molecule's volatility, scent and metabolism.

short: The largest class of plant natural products, built from five-carbon units; includes the essential-oil molecules, carnosic acid and ursolic acid.
definition: Terpenes are strictly hydrocarbons and terpenoids their oxygenated relatives, but the words are often used interchangeably.

short: A ten-carbon terpenoid; the main class of herb essential oils (menthol, thymol, linalool, 1,8-cineole, camphor, thujone).
definition: Monoterpenes are small, volatile and poorly soluble in water, which is why only a fraction reaches a tea.

short: A monoterpene carrying a C=O group, such as thujone, camphor, menthone and pulegone; several are the constituents of concern.
definition: Ketones in the catalogue have their own class label because several carry safety thresholds.

short: A fifteen-carbon terpenoid, made mainly in the cytosol: β-caryophyllene, α-bisabolol, chamazulene.
definition: Less volatile than monoterpenes, sesquiterpenes form the heavier notes of an oil.

short: A sesquiterpene with a lactone ring; common in the Asteraceae and a frequent cause of contact allergy.
definition: Sesquiterpene lactones help explain why Asteraceae allergies cross-react. The prototype does not profile one as a compound record.

short: A twenty-carbon terpenoid: carnosic acid and carnosol in rosemary and sage; teucrin A (a clerodane) in germander.
definition: Diterpenes are made in plastids from geranylgeranyl diphosphate and are generally not volatile.

short: A thirty-carbon terpenoid such as ursolic acid; waxy, insoluble in water and found in leaf surface wax.
definition: Pentacyclic triterpenes are made by cyclising 2,3-oxidosqualene and then oxidising the skeleton with P450 enzymes.

short: A compound derived from phenylalanine via cinnamic acid: eugenol, estragole, methyleugenol, caffeic and rosmarinic acid.
definition: The phenylpropanoid pathway also supplies lignin, coumarins and the flavonoids.

short: A small acid carrying a phenol ring, such as caffeic acid; rosmarinic acid is an ester of two of them. Water-soluble, so well extracted into tea.
definition: Phenolic acids are the main reason a hot-water infusion of a Lamiaceae herb is chemically different from its oil.

short: Loose term for plant compounds with several phenol rings (phenolic acids, flavonoids, tannins). Many are water-soluble; many are poorly absorbed.
definition: 'Total polyphenols' is a sum measured by a chemical assay, not a single compound, and is often given in gallic-acid equivalents.

short: A class of phenolics built from a phenylpropanoid unit plus three malonyl units: flavones, flavanones and more. Pigments, UV screens and signals in plants.
definition: In plants flavonoids occur mostly as glycosides; in the body they are heavily metabolised.

short: A subclass of flavonoids including apigenin, luteolin and the skullcap compounds baicalein and wogonin.
definition: Skullcap roots make unusual 4′-deoxyflavones (chrysin, wogonin, baicalein) by a root-specific pathway.

short: A flavonoid subclass without the 2,3 double bond of flavones; eriocitrin, peppermint tea's dominant phenolic, is a flavanone glycoside.
definition: Flavanones are intermediates on the way to flavones and other flavonoids.

short: A molecule with a sugar attached (a glucoside if the sugar is glucose). The sugar makes flavonoids water-soluble; it must be removed before absorption.
definition: Apigenin in chamomile and luteolin in thyme occur mainly as glycosides. Hot water extracts them well; gut enzymes cut the sugar off.

short: A molecule joined to glucuronic acid. Plants make some (baicalin, wogonoside, scutellarin); the human liver and gut make many more to excrete compounds.
definition: A compound measured in blood after eating a herb is often a glucuronide made by the body, not the plant's own form.

short: The non-sugar part of a glycoside: apigenin is the aglycone of apigenin-7-glucoside, baicalein of baicalin.
definition: Aglycones are less water-soluble than their glycosides but more readily absorbed across the gut wall.

short: Both a class of benzopyrone compounds (herniarin, umbelliferone) and one specific molecule, coumarin. The anticoagulant and liver cautions concern the specific molecule.
definition: Chamomile's herniarin and umbelliferone are coumarins in the class sense but are not the molecule coumarin; the teaching point is to keep the two senses apart.

short: A compound with several carbon-carbon triple bonds; chamomile's spiroethers belong here.
definition: Polyacetylenes are characteristic of the Asteraceae and Apiaceae and are often unstable to light and air.

short: A colourless precursor, such as matricin in chamomile, that turns into a blue azulene when heated in steam distillation.
definition: Proazulenes are why chamomile oil is blue while the flower and its tea are not.

short: A blue aromatic hydrocarbon skeleton; chamazulene, formed from matricin during distillation, gives chamomile oil its colour.
definition: Azulenes in an essential oil are largely artefacts of the distillation.

short: The volatile, fragrant fraction of a plant recovered by steam distillation: mostly monoterpenes, sesquiterpenes and phenylpropenes.
definition: An essential oil is a distillation product, not simply what is in the leaf; some constituents form during distillation and water-soluble compounds are absent. Oil capsules, tea and leaf are different test articles.

short: Passing steam through plant material and condensing it; the volatile oil separates from the water. It is how essential oils are made, and heat can create new molecules.
definition: Hydrodistillation boils the plant in water; steam distillation passes steam through it. Both recover volatiles and lose non-volatile phenolics.

short: Pouring hot water on plant material and letting it stand: a tea. It extracts water-soluble compounds well and volatile oil poorly.
definition: On this site an infusion is described as extraction chemistry (solvent water, a temperature, a time), never as a recipe or a dose.

short: Simmering plant material (usually roots or bark) in water, rather than steeping; longer and hotter than an infusion.
definition: Decoction is the traditional preparation of tough materials such as skullcap root. No study of what it extracts from S. baicalensis root was read for the prototype.

short: An extract made by soaking plant material in a mixture of ethanol and water. It reaches less polar compounds than water alone.
definition: Tinctures differ in herb-to-extract ratio, alcohol strength and fresh versus dried starting material, all of which change what they contain.

short: Made with a mixture of water and ethanol, such as a tincture or a 30-60 % ethanol extract.
definition: Mixtures extract both fairly polar phenolics and moderately non-polar compounds, which is why they often give the widest range.

short: How much plant went into how much finished extract, e.g. 1:5. It sets concentration but says nothing on its own about which compounds were extracted.
definition: A 70:1 dry extract is highly concentrated; a 1:5 tincture is dilute. Comparing extracts needs this ratio and the solvent.

short: How unevenly a molecule's electric charge is spread. Polar molecules (sugars, glycosides) dissolve in water; non-polar ones (terpenes) in oils and less-polar solvents.
definition: 'Like dissolves like' is the rule of thumb behind the difference between a tea, a tincture and an oil.

short: How much of a substance dissolves in a solvent at a given temperature; menthol is almost insoluble in water, glycosides dissolve readily.
definition: Solubility caps what an infusion can contain regardless of how much is in the leaf.

short: How readily a substance evaporates. Volatile oil molecules escape from hot water and from drying leaves; phenolics do not.
definition: Volatility is why a covered cup smells stronger and why some oil that dissolves is then lost to the air.

short: The share of a compound or fraction in the plant that ends up in the preparation, e.g. 31 % of lemon balm oil reaching the tea.
definition: A yield needs a denominator: the plant's content, or another extract used as the maximum. The figure on Tea Time keeps the two apart.

short: A rate law in which the amount still to be extracted falls exponentially with time: fast at first, then levelling off.
definition: Chamomile phenolics followed it, with the rate rising with water temperature; sage thujone saturated after about five minutes.

short: A capsule coated to survive stomach acid and release its contents in the intestine; the form of peppermint oil tested for irritable bowel symptoms.
definition: Enteric coating changes where and how much of the oil acts, which is one reason the capsule evidence does not transfer to tea. Antacids can dissolve the coating early.

short: A protein that a signalling molecule binds to, triggering a response in the cell; the named molecular target of a compound.
definition: A compound binding a receptor in vitro is grade E evidence of a mechanism, not evidence of an effect after drinking a tea.

short: A molecule that binds a receptor and activates it, as menthol activates the cold receptor TRPM8.
definition: Partial agonists activate less than fully; potency and efficacy are separate properties.

short: A molecule that binds a receptor or channel and blocks its activation, as α-thujone blocks the GABA-A receptor's chloride channel.
definition: Blocking an inhibitory receptor such as GABA-A makes neurons more excitable, which is the basis of thujone's convulsant toxicity.

short: The brain's main inhibitory ion channel, opened by GABA. Thujone blocks it (convulsant); benzodiazepines bind a separate site on it.
definition: Benzodiazepine drugs such as diazepam bind a separate pocket on the receptor, the benzodiazepine site, and enhance its response to GABA. Apigenin's reported binding to that site is laboratory evidence; its low bioavailability limits what it implies for chamomile tea.

short: An ion channel in sensory nerves that opens at cool temperatures and when menthol binds; why mint feels cold.
definition: Its cloning in 2002 gave menthol's cooling a single molecular explanation.

short: A cannabinoid receptor found mainly on immune cells; β-caryophyllene binds it selectively in laboratory studies.
definition: CB2 activation does not produce the psychoactive effects of the CB1 receptor.

short: Organic anion-transporting polypeptides: transporters that carry drugs such as statins into liver cells. Baicalin altered rosuvastatin exposure via OATP1B1.
definition: Transporter interactions are a second route to herb-drug interactions besides P450 enzymes.

short: The fraction of an ingested compound that reaches the bloodstream unchanged. Many plant polyphenols have very low bioavailability.
definition: Low bioavailability is the usual gap between a striking in-vitro result and any effect in people. Metabolites, not the plant's own form, are often what circulates.

short: Metabolism of a swallowed compound by the gut wall and liver before it reaches general circulation; it can remove most of a dose.
definition: Glucuronidation and sulfation in the gut and liver are major first-pass routes for flavonoids. Some conjugates are excreted in bile, split again by gut bacteria and reabsorbed (enterohepatic recycling, reported for apigenin), which prolongs exposure.

short: When one substance changes the effect or blood level of another, e.g. by inhibiting the enzyme or transporter that handles it.
definition: Each interaction in the safety blocks carries its own grade: many rest on animal or laboratory data.

short: A multi-herb Japanese kampo formula containing S. baicalensis root; linked to interstitial pneumonitis and liver injury reports.
definition: Its evidence belongs to the formula; this site does not transfer it to skullcap alone.

short: A compound with a known hazard or a regulatory threshold (thujone, pulegone, estragole, methyleugenol). Always curated, regardless of abundance.
definition: Each appears in the safety block of every plant and preparation that contains it, with the relevant limit and its source.

short: Damage to the liver caused by a chemical. Reported for germander (teucrin A), pulegone and some skullcap products.
definition: Most herbal liver injury is rare and idiosyncratic, and adulteration can make a harmless herb look guilty.

short: Conversion of a harmless-looking compound into a reactive, toxic one by the body's own enzymes, often cytochrome P450.
definition: Pulegone (to menthofuran and beyond), estragole (1′-hydroxylation then sulfoconjugation) and teucrin A (furan oxidation) are all toxic only after bioactivation.

short: Able to damage DNA, for example by forming DNA adducts. A genotoxic carcinogen is assumed to have no fully safe threshold.
definition: That assumption is why the EMA sets very low guidance values for estragole and advises minimising methyleugenol exposure.

short: Causes cancer in rats or mice at the doses tested. Estragole and methyleugenol are rodent carcinogens; that is a hazard, not a measured human risk.
definition: Rodent studies use doses far above dietary exposure; regulators extrapolate with safety factors.

short: Substitution or contamination of a herbal product with another plant. Some liver injury blamed on skullcap was traced to germander.
definition: Analytical methods can now distinguish Scutellaria from Teucrium, which is why identity is treated as part of safety.

short: Teucrium, a mint-family genus whose diterpenoid teucrin A causes liver injury; a known adulterant of skullcap.
definition: Germander was withdrawn from use in France after a series of hepatitis cases in the 1990s.

short: An allergy to one substance causing reactions to related ones: ragweed-allergic people may react to chamomile.
definition: Cross-reactivity within the Asteraceae and, more rarely, the Lamiaceae is part of the safety blocks.

short: A severe, rapid, whole-body allergic reaction that can be fatal; rare reports exist with chamomile.
definition: Listed in the EU chamomile monograph among hypersensitivity reactions.

short: A substance that causes an allergic skin reaction where it touches; carnosol is a major rosemary contact allergen.
definition: Contact allergy is a skin-sensitisation effect and says nothing about drinking a tea.

short: Able to cause seizures. Thujone and camphor are convulsant at high doses; the EMA thujone limit is based on rodent seizure data.
definition: Case reports include a toddler's seizure after home-made sage tea; these are why sage carries a safety block.

short: A reflex stop in breathing (with spasm of the larynx) that menthol near the face can trigger in infants; why menthol oils are contraindicated under 2 years.
definition: Recorded in the EU peppermint-oil monograph.

short: A condition in which a product should not be used, as stated in a monograph, e.g. hypersensitivity or age under 2 years for menthol oils.
definition: Contraindications are reported as the monograph's statement, not as the site's advice.

short: The convulsant monoterpenoid ketone of sage (two isomers, α and β); blocks the GABA-A receptor. EMA sets daily exposure values for it.
definition: In sage tea thujone rises for about five minutes and then levels off; a water infusion recovers only part of what ethanol extracts.

short: A monoterpenoid ketone of mints that is hepatotoxic after bioactivation; limited by the EMA together with menthofuran.
definition: Pulegone is an intermediate on peppermint's pathway to menthol; the Ph. Eur. caps it in peppermint oil.

short: A furan-containing monoterpene in peppermint oil and a major metabolite of pulegone; counted with pulegone under the EMA limit.
definition: Its furan ring is oxidised in the liver to reactive products.

short: The aniseed-scented phenylpropene of some basils; a genotoxic carcinogen in rodents with an EMA guidance value of 0.05 mg per person per day.
definition: Its level ranges from minor to dominant between basil chemotypes, which is why the basil page shows ranges.

short: A clove-like phenylpropene in most basil cultivars grown here; a rodent genotoxic carcinogen. The EMA gives no number but advises minimising exposure.
definition: Made from eugenol by an O-methyltransferase in basil's glandular trichomes.

short: A chemically distinct form within one species, e.g. thymol-type versus other thyme, or estragole-rich versus linalool-rich basil. Same plant name, different oil.
definition: Chemotypes are genetic, often traceable to single enzymes, and are why a species-level percentage can mislead about a particular plant.

short: A common gut disorder of abdominal pain and altered bowel habit; the condition in the peppermint-oil capsule trials.
definition: Named here only to identify the trial populations behind a grade, never as a recommendation. (The lemon balm cream trial, similarly, was in cold sores - herpes labialis - with a concentrated 70:1 dry extract as the test article.)

short: A condition of persistent excessive worry; the population of the chamomile-extract trials.
definition: Named to identify the trial population behind a grade; the test article was a chamomile extract in capsules, not tea.
